scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

This year, as you fast or pray, you’re not just *remembering* that; you’re actively practicing patience in real time, because the ritual has trained your awareness. Over 10 years? That awareness becomes instinctive. - Psychology calls this **"neural pruning"**— the more you revisit a thought ( like " I owe others compassion"), the stronger those pathways become. What starts as a conscious effort becomes a reflex. - Theologically, this aligns with St. Paul’s idea of " being transformed by the renewing of your mind" ( Romans 12:2). Rituals aren’t just about * doing*; they’re about * becoming*. --- ### 2. ** the " same thing" is a mirror, not a script** It’s easy to think annual traditions are repetitive or predictable—but in reality, ** the " same" ritual reveals * different* layers of your heart each time.** - Year 1: Lent might focus on " I need to forgive my siblings for past arguments." - Year 5: It might uncover " I’m holding onto resentment I didn’t even know I had toward my parents." - Year 10: It could shift to " I owe others not just forgiveness, but active advocacy for their dignity." - This is why Lent * feels* fresh every year, even if the structure is familiar. The ritual isn’t static; * you* are growing. The " 40 days of fasting" isn’t just about giving up chocolate—it’s a sacred space to * see* yourself more clearly, year after year. - As theologian Rowan Williams wrote: " Rituals are not about repeating the past; they’re about * making the past present* in a way that transforms the future." --- ### 3. ** " what we owe others" is reframed by community** You mention doing this " with family and church"— and that’s critical. ** Rituals aren’t solitary.** They’re communal acts that remind us we’re part of something larger than ourselves. - When your church community gathers for Ash Wednesday, or your family light Advent candles together, you’re not just * thinking* about " what I owe others"— you’re * enacting* it. You see others’ struggles, share their burdens, and realize: " I don’t owe others abstractly; I owe them * this* ( my time, my silence, my hands to help)." - In Christian tradition, this is called ** " koinonia"**— shared life. The more you practice it annually, the more " what I owe others" shifts from a guilt-driven obligation to a joyful participation in a shared story of grace. - *Example*: A family that fasts together during Lent doesn’t just * talk* about hunger; they might donate the money saved to a food bank. Year after year, that action becomes part of their identity. " Owing others" becomes " * being* for others." --- ### 4. ** the danger ( and the antidote) of " going through the motions"** You’re right to worry about rituals becoming empty. But here’s the beautiful thing: ** your awareness of it is the antidote.** - If you ever feel like Lent is " just a routine," that’s actually a sign your heart is awake. Ask: " What is this year’s * specific* invitation for me? Who do I need to forgive * today*? How can I * see* the person I’ve been ignoring?" - as the mystic Thomas Merton wrote: " The purpose of Lent is not to * remember* Christ’s suffering, but to * enter* it— so that we might * become* Christ for others." --- ### in short: ** yes, annual rituals change how you see what you owe others—but not because they’re " the same." They change you because they’re * different* each time, because * you* are different each time.** - Christmas and Easter aren’t just " holidays"; they’re * anchors* in time that pull you back to what matters most: love, grace, and the radical idea that we’re all connected. - Lent’s 40 days aren’t a punishment; they’re a * gift*— a yearly invitation to " unlearn" self-centeredness and " relearn" how to see others as Christ sees them. - Over time, that doesn’t just change your * thoughts* about what you owe others; it changes your * heart* so that " owing others" feels less like a duty and more like a natural response to being loved first. You’re already doing the work by being mindful of it. That’s the most important part. The ritual isn’t the change agent— * your attention to it* is. And that’s why these traditions endure: they’re not about " what we * do"* but about " who we * become." Thank you for sharing this.
